structure.title: Producing and distributing wealth
structure.text: The opening examines divided labour, exchange, prices, and income, then the accumulation and use of capital.

structure.title: Systems and government
structure.text: Later books consider historical development, competing economic policies, and public expenditure and revenue.

people.name: Division of labour
people.text: Smith's opening example: ten workers in a pin factory, each doing one step, make thousands of times more pins than they could alone.

people.name: Capital
people.text: The stock of savings put to work, which Smith argues sets how much productive labour a country can employ and so how fast it can grow.

people.name: Monopoly
people.text: Exclusive rights granted to merchants and companies, which Smith attacks for raising prices and serving a few at the public's expense.

context.title: Political economy
context.text: Smith examines production within laws, institutions, and social relations. The book is broader than a defence of unregulated buying and selling.

context.title: Historical vocabulary
context.text: Terms such as stock and productive labour have particular uses within Smith's account. Modern everyday meanings can mislead.
context.takeaway: Learn the local definition before judging a claim.

notice.why: Private interest can work against the public benefits of competition.
Rising output does not answer every question about a good society.

opening: A pin is an insignificant object until Adam Smith looks at how it is made. Dividing the work lets a small group produce quantities no individual could approach, and that observation opens onto the wealth of entire societies. Smith follows labour, trade, prices, and government through the arrangements that fill a dinner table. He also watches merchants seek privileges and workers bear the costs of progress. The economy becomes a human construction whose remarkable productivity offers no guarantee that its rewards will be shared fairly.
